newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire shuts flashpoint campuses, fear grips city.
newsitem.headline: Zaire shuts flashpoint campuses, fear grips city.

text.p: Zaire on Monday shut two Kinshasa campuses spearheading violent protests against government handling of a Tutsi rebellion.
But shops, petrol stations and some businesses closed, fearing further trouble in the capital, witnesses said.
Troops forced students from their beds in the dead of night and smashed roadblocks the students had erected in parts of the capital for the past week, the witnesses said.
Student violence, including the hijacking of private cars and other vehicles, has left the sprawling city of more than five million people without transport.
Streets surged with people as commuters hurried home on foot with bus and taxi operators too scared to venture out.

Residents said the students, many of whom are allied to radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, were trying to regroup to press their campaign against the government and Rwanda, which Zaire accuses of aiding ethnic Tutsis.

The radical opposition commands a strong following in the capital and many Zaireans are angered by their army's poor showing on the battlefield. Yet residents largely resent the student action because of the hardship it has brought on a city with no real public services.
Students are demanding $500 from owners before releasing commandeered vehicles, residents said.

Banyamulenge Tutsis have overwhelmed the Zaire army in two provinces bordering Rwanda since fighting erupted on October 18. About 1.2 million Rwandan and Burundian refugees in camps and hundreds of thousands of Zairean villagers have been displaced.

Students briefly occupied parliament last week, demanding the resignation of part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo. They urged people to stay away from work and close their shops in a "ghost town" protest on Monday.

"At this moment when we have been invaded by Rwanda, Zaire needs a strong government which has the confidence of both the civilian population and the armed forces," leading student activist Steve Mbikayi told Reuters.
"It is not with an impotent government that we'll chase out the enemy," he added.

The government last week ordered the closure of the campuses of the Institute of Applied Technology and the Institutue of Commerce. Hundreds of troops from the civil guard and gendamerie moved in at 3. a.m. and scattered students into the night.
By daybreak the crumbling residence halls and lecture rooms were deserted apart from soldiers on guard outside.
"Many of the students are from outside Kinshasa and have no homes to go to. They are gathering with their belongings at a cathedral in town," said Jean d'Oliveira, a public relations consultant.
Student leader Mbikayi said the government's closure of the colleges was illegitimate because even the professors and lecturers were no longer paid by the bankrupt state.

Student protesters have targeted Tutsi property and accused the government of doing too little to help the army, which has lost control of a string of towns in the eastern refugee provinces, including Goma and Bukavu.

Zaire accuses Tutsi-led Rwanda of fomenting the revolt in the east and of invading its territory. Rwanda, which had accused Rwandan Hutu hardliners of using the region as a springboard for raids into its territory, denies the charge.
